extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and editors (cub reporters, city editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical newsroom guidance on writing leads, reporting court and police news, and avoiding libel — including what is privileged, how to attribute, and when truth or retraction will protect the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Court leads need not always be the same; when many cases are heard the reporter can either (1) lead with the single most interesting/important case and then mention or summarize other cases, or (2) use a summary lead that mentions no specific cases or names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: a name lead that gives the most interesting case first and then others in subsequent paragraphs; or a summary lead such as 'Jail sentences totaling eight years and fines amounting to $265 were imposed yesterday.' Choose the form based on the day's cases and headline considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order consistency between lead and story
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever cases are mentioned, whether by summary or by name, in the lead should be detailed in the order of presentation in the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining the same sequence gives the story an obvious structure and makes it easier for readers to follow rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider headline consequences ('name head')
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter should consider the sort of headline a story will receive and whether the offense justifies a 'name head' (naming the accused in the headline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'name head' can be unduly severe relative to the offense (e.g., a thirty-point headline may punish more than a small fine). Avoid name heads for technical offenses that may not warrant public shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use summary lead when many 'technically guilty' cases appear
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary lead (mentioning no names) emphasizes the court rather than the accused and is appropriate when the strongest part of the court news consists of cases that are technically but not morally guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form reduces undue focus on individuals whose guilt may be technical or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know libel law as both protection and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must understand libel law and keep up with changes: it restricts what can be printed but also marks off things the paper may lawfully do and thus protects the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law changes by statute and court decisions; journalists should consult trade publications (e.g., Editor & Publisher) and not rely solely on desk editors or folk rules of thumb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is a defense — but must be provable to a jury
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement generally isn't libelous if you can prove it was true so well that a jury believes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing a fact isn't enough; the newspaper must be able to present convincing proof (official court records, etc.). Even true facts can be legally risky if a jury won't accept them.

rubrics_metrics.name: In some states truth requires 'good motives'
rubrics_metrics.description: In a few states the mere truth of a statement is not a complete defense; the motives for publishing must also be good (truth plus worthy motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites specific examples (Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, West Virginia, Illinois, Nebraska). This affects decision-making about printing old or potentially scandalous truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of libel — public ridicule, hatred, or contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: The law says you damage a person when what you print holds them up to public ridicule, hatred, or contempt; these are the three recognized ways to harm reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test to think about whether published characterizations reduce a person's standing in public esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel per se vs. libel per quod
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statements are libelous on their face (libel per se) — e.g., calling someone a criminal or a prostitute. Other statements become libelous because of special circumstances (libel per quod) — e.g., saying someone 'went to the Red Rooster' when that place is known locally as a brothel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either way, truth is a defense if it can be proved; absent proof the statement is libelous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer's intent is secondary to reader's interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: What the public believes the writer meant counts more than the writer's actual intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous, humorous, or 'smart' phrasing that readers could reasonably interpret as defamatory (example: a phrasing that implies illegal operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper is responsible for accuracy regardless of source
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper is responsible for what it prints even when the error originated from a police source, telegraph company, or correspondent; the newspaper may have to pay damages for mistakes by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: relying on state police who were wrong; telegraph name-twisting; a reporter should verify names and facts. Desk editors cannot absolve the reporter's responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification without naming can be libelous
rubrics_metrics.description: A person or business may be libeled even without being named if sufficient identifying detail (location, description) allows readers to identify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: describing the store location where a child died of suspected impure ice cream was enough to identify the storekeeper and would have exposed the paper to a libel suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, impartiality, and completeness for privileged reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of courts and legislatures are conditionally privileged only if they are accurate, impartial, and complete — especially 'complete' in the sense of presenting both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a multi-day case is reported only from the prosecution's side on one day (dropping defense coverage), the immunity may be lost. 'Complete' does not mean printing every detail, but presenting both sides sufficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional privilege — meet the tests to claim immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of 'conditional privilege' means the newspaper's immunity for reporting certain public matters exists only if specifications of accuracy, impartiality, and completeness are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is also 'absolute privilege' in limited contexts, but reporters should rely on meeting the conditional privilege tests for routine court/legislative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege for official communications and proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Official communications of military/naval officers, Presidents or governors, and official proceedings of public boards and commissions are privileged matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These official reports may be published without fear of libel so long as they are handled as public, official material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand jury testimony and privilege limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony given before a grand jury (held in camera) is not privileged and may expose the newspaper to contempt; only formal reports of indictments released by the grand jury are privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should not publish grand jury testimony except when officially released.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications of damages and retraction value
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages fall into nominal, compensatory, and punitive categories. A prompt, sincere, and prominent retraction can mitigate damages but is not a cure-all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominal damages vindicate character (small amounts). Compensatory recompense for real harm (lost job). Punitive awarded for malicious or reckless conduct. Retractions vary by state in protective power and generally serve as mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police news: only recorded facts privileged; police reasoning is not
rubrics_metrics.description: The law permits publication of recorded parts of police news (statement of arrest and charge). The police's reasoning, suspicions, and investigative detail are not privileged and can be libelous if printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure: first paragraph stating the arrest and charge is safe; follow-up paragraphs that relay police suspicions or unverified detective opinions risk libel if the accused is later acquitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute ex parte or prejudiced statements to their source and emphasize opinion status
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing information that is not part of the official record (ex parte police statements or opinions), the paper should attribute those statements to the police or source and emphasize that they are the source's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'Police declare' or 'Lieut. Mahoney said' show the paper's good faith and may reduce the appearance of malice, though they do not eliminate libel risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualify doubtful identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If identity is uncertain, the reporter should qualify the identification (e.g., 'the driver identified himself as John Doe, 211 Zero Street').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice reduces the paper's exposure when a supposed identification later proves incorrect (examples of borrowed cars and mixed-up registration/permits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit speculation beyond official filings until the case is before the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing of a lawsuit with the clerk is 'official' to the extent of stating that a suit was entered, but details about allegations should not be printed as fact until the case is actually before the court (judge's consideration) unless state law treats filing as bringing the case before the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State variations: New York and Kentucky (by precedent) and Ohio (by statute) consider a case before the court upon filing; elsewhere details aren't privileged until the judge enters the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wording that implies professional incompetence or moral failing
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful word choice is required to avoid implying professional incompetence or moral turpitude (e.g., don't write someone 'died of an operation' which suggests surgeon's clumsiness; instead write 'died after an operation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, avoid wrongly asserting incompetence, financial instability, or unpalatable sickness which would lower public esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of damaging characterizations to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that a person is criminal, a prostitute, incompetent, lacking integrity or financial stability, or afflicted with stigmatizing disease are damaging and potentially libelous if untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution before publishing characterizations that strike at a person's respectability; consider both literal wording and contextual implications.
